content: The search strategy for PAIS International was originally conducted in January 2015, with the search date recorded as January 14, 2014. A total of 375 records were identified across all years. The search was performed using ProQuest, and the search terms were structured to include various combinations of keywords related to housing, indoor environments, and thermal conditions. The search terms included variations of house, houses, housing, home, homes, residence, building, accommodation, shelter, and slum, combined with terms related to ventilation, air conditioning, humidity, heating, and temperature. These terms were searched in both the abstract (ab) and title (ti) fields. Additionally, the search strategy incorporated terms related to indoor temperature, heat exposure, heatwaves, hot spells, and thermal stress, as well as domestic temperature and air conditioning. The search also included terms like cooling, ventilation, and insulation, combined with the housing-related terms mentioned earlier. The search was further refined to include terms like increase, raise, elevate, susceptibility, and ambient, in proximity to temperature or heat. These terms were also searched in both the abstract and title fields. The systematic review aimed to identify literature on indoor heat exposure and its implications for the WHO Housing and Health Guidelines. The search strategy was comprehensive, covering multiple databases and using a wide range of keywords to ensure the inclusion of relevant studies. The search was also conducted in the Science Citation Index via the Web of Science, with a search date of January 14, 2015. A total of 5,283 records were retrieved, spanning the time period from 1900 to 2015. The search terms in this database included similar combinations of keywords related to housing, temperature, heat, and indoor environmental conditions. The search strategy was designed to capture studies on the effects of indoor heat, ventilation, air conditioning, and other thermal factors on housing and health. The results were systematically reviewed to inform the development of the WHO Housing and Health Guidelines.
